Christoffel distribution and sampling¶

This page describes the Christoffel distribution associated with an approximation space, the determinantal point processes (DPP) built on the Christoffel kernel, and the sampling strategies of the ChristoffelSubsampleExperiment. Throughout, denotes the number of design points and the dimension of the approximation space, as in the API. This is the opposite of the convention of [cohendolbeault2020], where is the number of points and the space dimension.

Christoffel distribution¶

The Christoffel distribution is the probability measure on defined by

(4)¶

The trace identity (3) shows that is a probability measure. It is the reference measure tilted by the pointwise energy of the approximation space: the density of is large where the basis functions are large, so that Christoffel samples concentrate where the space has the largest pointwise influence. For the uniform measure on and the Legendre basis, for example, the density concentrates at the endpoints of the interval. For the arcsine measure and the Chebyshev basis, the ratio stays bounded between two positive constants, so remains comparable to without endpoint concentration.

The Christoffel measure is the optimal importance sampling measure for least squares. Let be any probability measure on such that is absolutely continuous with respect to , with Radon-Nikodym derivative . A design is a set of points together with weights, : the points are drawn from , and are importance weights that map -expectations back to . They are not replication counts or classical design weights; when , all the weights are one. Keeping the points and the weights in a single object lets the same design define the quadrature rule, the weighted least squares estimator, and the Gramian (6) below.

The factor is the price of conditioning on the certified event. The conditioned estimator, which sets the estimate to zero outside instead of normalizing by , only gives the weaker bound with an additional term. The sampling error is thus a small multiplicative factor over the best possible error; for a fixed confidence level and growing , the -dependent term tends to zero. The inequality also shows why the Christoffel measure is optimal: it makes as small as possible, hence the budget as small as possible.

The ChristoffelSubsampleExperiment uses the largest integer such that when its certified mode is enabled. This is the leading-order form of (9), where the term is omitted. The experiment then draws independent points from , computes the weights (5), and checks the realized frame (7) with the default tolerance (the ChristoffelSubsampleExperiment-FrameTolerance key). If the realized design misses the band, the whole independent sample is redrawn, up to the number of attempts set by the ChristoffelSubsampleExperiment-MaxAttempts key. When no attempt passes, the experiment returns the draw whose weighted Gramian has the largest smallest eigenvalue, that is the sharpest realized frame among the attempts, and warns with the frame bounds of that retained design. The theorem gives the probability scale of the budget; the frame check turns it into an operational certificate for the realized design.

This certified sizing fixes and adapts . It is natural when the approximation space belongs to a nested hierarchy and can be chosen freely. In many applications, is fixed by the model and only the number of evaluations can be adapted; the certificate should then be read in the other direction, as the lower bound for the fixed . The current API exposes the fixed- strategy only; a fixed- strategy, which would choose from , is left for a future release. As a workaround, choose the smallest target size whose certified dimension is the fixed , for (and for ), provided the basis supplies functions and . For small the formula can give ; the certified dimension is then bounded by , so check getSpaceDimension() and increase (or ) until it is . This inherits the leading-order confidence of the certified sizing.

The default mode of the experiment does not use this sizing: it chooses as the largest dimension supplied by the basis, which gives a much larger approximation space for the same budget but no certified frame guarantee. The frame check is then advisory only, and the design is returned after a single draw: if it misses the band, the caller should reduce the space dimension (by truncating the basis or switching to certified sizing) or, when the basis capacity keeps fixed, increase . The experiment does not redraw in this mode: it returns the first draw without retrying, even though the realized miss still depends on the sampled points. Retrying is reserved for the certified mode, where the independent budget makes the probability statement meaningful. The trade-off is the classical one between a square design (as many points as basis functions) and an overdetermined certified design (more points than basis functions, with a guaranteed stability margin).

Determinantal point processes on the Christoffel kernel¶

A determinantal point process on with kernel is a point process whose joint intensities with respect to are determinants of the kernel [macchi1975], [hough2009]:

(12)¶

For the Christoffel kernel of (1), which is a projection kernel of rank , the DPP has exactly points almost surely. The law of the points is exchangeable, with joint density

(13)¶

with respect to ; the normalization follows from the Andreief identity and the trace identity (3). The density is invariant under permutation of the points: it describes the set of points rather than a distinguished ordering. The one-point intensity with respect to is , so the expected number of points is . Normalized by the number of points, each ordered coordinate, and hence , has density

and its Lebesgue density is .

A DPP sample is therefore marginally Christoffel-distributed, but the points are not independent. The pair intensity is

(14)¶

with a strict inequality as soon as . This negative dependence, or repulsion, is the defining feature of a DPP: points avoid each other, and coincident points have probability zero for a continuous . Repulsion is precisely what a design of experiments needs: a DPP sample is spread over the support instead of clumping as an independent sample would. DPP samples are also used directly as Monte Carlo quadrature rules, with a variance controlled by the kernel [bardenet2020].

The DPP also has a volume interpretation. Let be the matrix whose rows are . Since is a projection kernel,

(15)¶

The probability of a configuration is thus proportional to the squared volume of the -parallelotope spanned by its feature vectors. This volume interpretation connects the projection DPP with volume sampling, the subset-selection rule discussed below; continuous formulations of volume sampling, including versions with repetitions, are studied in [nouymichel2025]. It favors configurations with a large volume, hence well-spread feature vectors and a well-conditioned feature matrix. Repulsion acts on the feature vectors, not on the ambient distance: two points can be far apart in while producing nearly collinear features, and they then repel each other strongly; conversely, nearly orthogonal feature vectors correspond to weak repulsion. In the univariate polynomial case, the projection DPP is the orthogonal polynomial ensemble associated with [hough2009], the random matrix model whose eigenvalues have the same Christoffel kernel.

Sequential sampling¶

A projection DPP can be sampled exactly and sequentially. Suppose that points have already been accepted, with feature matrix (one row per accepted point) and Gram matrix . For a candidate , define

The residual kernel after the accepted points is

(16)¶

and its diagonal is the squared residual norm of the feature vector of after projection onto the span of the accepted features. The conditional density of the next point is proportional to with respect to , with normalizing constant , because the residual kernel has rank and trace .

The implementation proposes a candidate from the Christoffel distribution , whose density is , and accepts it with probability

(17)¶

The acceptance probability is not the full target over proposal ratio: the latter would be . The missing constant cancels in the normalization of the rejection sampler, so (17) is exact and, unlike the full ratio, never exceeds one. The expected number of proposals for the -th point is , and the expected total number of proposals is

where is the -th harmonic number. Each accepted point requires a rank-one update of the inverse Gram matrix (a Sherman-Morrison update in the implementation), so the dense sequential sampler has a cost that grows quickly with ; this is why the experiment is intended for moderate space dimensions. The implementation also guards against non-finite or numerically zero residuals, which can occur when a candidate is numerically in the span of the accepted points.

Conditional DPP and volume sampling¶

Two variants are used when the design must reuse already computed points.

Conditional DPP. Let be a set of supplied points with linearly independent feature vectors, and let be their feature matrix. Conditionally on these points being part of the DPP, the remaining points follow a DPP with the residual kernel

(18)¶

This is the same residual kernel as in (16), with the fixed points playing the role of the accepted points. Conditioning is possible only for at most supplied points; more than points cannot be conditioned on because the projection kernel has rank , and the feature vectors of supplied points must be linearly independent for to be invertible.

Volume sampling from a candidate set. Let be a candidate set with , drawn from the reference measure , and let be its feature vectors. Volume sampling selects a subset of size with probability

(19)¶

where is the matrix of the selected feature vectors. When , this is the projection-DPP law restricted to the finite pool, written as volume sampling. This finite-pool law is not a continuous Christoffel sample: the selected points do not inherit the continuous Christoffel marginals, and is not in general an unbiased quadrature weight for . Those properties require the continuous projection-DPP or volume-rescaled constructions, where the determinant is defined by the reference measure rather than by a finite pool, or a pool whose empirical Gram matrix is the identity. When , the selection is the identity: all candidates are kept and, since no Christoffel selection has taken place, they are returned with unit weights as a plain Monte Carlo sample of . When , the determinant is positive exactly when the selected feature vectors span the -dimensional space. By the Cauchy-Binet identity it equals the sum over all -subsets of the squared volume of the -parallelotope spanned by that subset; volume sampling extends the DPP construction by favoring subsets whose span has a large volume [derezinski2021]. It is the natural way to recycle a larger pool of already evaluated points, and it is exact, not a heuristic thinning. Volume sampling is not restricted to finite candidate sets: continuous volume-rescaled formulations, with their own Christoffel-marginal and quadrature guarantees, are also available [nouymichel2025].

The implementation draws the volume sample by reverse removal. With candidates remaining, the leverage score of candidate is

where is the current feature matrix. Since , removing candidate with probability proportional to yields exactly the volume distribution (19) after removals. The Gramian inverse and the leverage scores are updated by Sherman-Morrison after each removal, with a periodic exact refresh to control round-off errors. A zero removal probability signals a numerically rank-deficient candidate set and is rejected.

Mixing a DPP with independent points. In the default square mode with , the first points form a projection DPP and the remaining points are independent draws from . The union is not a DPP: the independent part adds no repulsion, and the two blocks are not exchangeable. The experiment randomly permutes the design so that the returned ordering does not expose the blocks, and it checks the frame only as an advisory diagnostic. The DPP block is a continuous volume-rescaled sample of size with base [derezinski2021]. The full design is not standard volume-rescaled sampling of size , because the independent points do not enter a determinant. More general schemes draw the independent points from another measure chosen to guarantee almost-sure bounds, or repeat the DPP block; both are studied in [nouymichel2025], where repetitions are observed to be more effective than independent filling, although no theoretical guarantee that they are always better is available yet.

Sampling the Christoffel distribution¶

The Christoffel distribution is the reference measure tilted by , and its support is the support of . The implementation provides two sampling paths, described in ChristoffelDistribution.

Tensor-product reference measure. When is a product measure with independent marginals, , and the basis is a tensor product of univariate functions, the Christoffel density factorizes conditionally. Write a basis function as , where is a multi-index. Given the first coordinates, the conditional density of is

(20)¶

This conditional density is sampled by rejection. A bounded marginal uses a uniform proposal on its numerical range and an envelope of the target density. An unbounded marginal uses a two-sided Cauchy proposal, or a half-Cauchy proposal for a one-sided support, because the polynomial factor gives the Christoffel density heavier tails than the reference measure: truncating at the numerical range would bias high-degree samples. The envelope is scanned on a grid uniform in the proposal CDF, which resolves narrow peaks near the mode, and multiplied by a safety factor. A proposal that exceeds the envelope raises it and is discarded, so the sampler never accepts a proposal above the envelope. As for any rejection sampler, exactness is conditional on the envelope bounding the target-to-proposal ratio everywhere: the scan is a numerical estimate, not a proof of the supremum, so a peak missed by the grid can bias the sample. Since an accepted draw is final, raising the envelope after a later exceedance cannot correct a draw accepted under an earlier, too low envelope.

Other reference measures. When the tensor-product structure is not available, the class compares two samplers before generating and keeps the one with the larger measured acceptance rate. The first is rejection from the reference measure with the envelope , an estimate of over the numerical range obtained from a low-discrepancy candidate pool and refined by a bounded multi-start maximization of the log-Christoffel function, with a safety factor. Rejection accepts with probability . The second is the internal ratio-of-uniforms sampler [stadlober1990]. A setup failure at any dimension falls back to rejection. The stability factor carries a safety margin, the rejection sampler raises its envelope and discards the offending proposal whenever one exceeds it, and the ratio-of-uniforms sampler rejects every proposal that violates its bounds. As on the tensor path, rejection is exact only when the envelope bounds the density ratio: the stability factor remains a numerical estimate, and a later exceedance cannot correct an earlier accepted draw. The ratio-of-uniforms sampler operates on the numerical range, so it is exact for a bounded reference whose range covers the support and can truncate the tails of an unbounded non-tensor reference; use the tensor path for unbounded product measures.

Two numerical cautions are worth stating. First, the interval returned by getRange() is a numerical range, not necessarily the support: for an unbounded reference it stores extreme quantiles, and the PDF may be positive outside that interval. The tensor sampler does not truncate an unbounded marginal to the numerical range, while the ratio-of-uniforms branch is set up on that range. Second, a reference density that underflows to zero makes the PDF zero even when the reference log-density is finite; the log-PDF and the log-Christoffel function are the stable entry points in the tails.

Orthonormality is a precondition. The Christoffel function is a density factor only when the basis is orthonormal with respect to . The classes do not check this condition and do not orthogonalize the basis. A cheap numerical check is the trace identity (3), for example the empirical mean of computeChristoffelFunction() over a sample of , which must be close to . For a correlated reference measure, tensor-orthonormal functions must be composed with a whitening map of before being passed to the basis: for a multivariate normal with mean and covariance , use . The uncentered map applies only when ; the correlation matrix may replace the covariance in when the marginals are standardized. When the input is a raw dictionary, a quasi-orthogonalization pre-step is therefore recommended before constructing the Christoffel distribution: orthogonalize the dictionary with respect to , for example by Gram-Schmidt or by a Cholesky factorization of its Gram matrix, and monitor the conditioning of the transformation. Optimal sampling and quasi-orthogonalization for general dictionaries are analyzed in [trunschkenouy2025].
